research_question: What evidence-based connection exists between JANUS BIOPAPYRUS, ancient Egyptian oil extraction/pressing, ancient Egyptian oil vocabulary, and modern bacterial-cellulose interaction with oils?

MORINGA_OR_OLIVE_OIL.meaning: oil of the moringa tree (?) or olive oil (?)

PRESS_OUT_OIL.meaning: to press out oil; to cook unguent

MIDDLE_KINGDOM_PRESS_RELIEF.description: Relief fragment showing a wine/oil press: a sack in a net is tightened with a lever until liquid is squeezed out; the museum notes the scene may represent perfume production from flowers soaked in oil.

ARCHAEOBOTANICAL_OIL_SOURCES.summary: Vegetable oils/fats are chemically identified in some residues. Linseed was grown in Egypt from early times; moringa nuts and balanos kernels are plausible oil sources; olive and possibly sesame appear to have been imported and likely were not grown in Egypt before the New Kingdom or later.

shared_mechanical_primitive.JANUS_BIOPAPYRUS: PRESS / flatten a wet cellulose sheet while removing liquid
shared_mechanical_primitive.ANCIENT_OIL_EXTRACTION: PRESS / compress plant or infused material to force liquid oil/perfumed liquid out

process_bridge.important_difference: In oil extraction the desired product is usually the expelled liquid; in BioPapyrus the desired product is the densified cellulose sheet. The same mechanical primitive is used with opposite product priorities.

oil_and_bacterial_cellulose_bridge.baseline: Bacterial cellulose is strongly hydrophilic and its properties change with moisture; oil interaction is therefore a measurable material variable, not automatically a protective finish.
supported_modern_context: Bacterial-cellulose membranes are used in oil/water-separation research because their wet surfaces can be hydrophilic and underwater oleophobic.
Bacterial cellulose can be chemically or physically modified with hydrophobic agents; fatty-acid/wax treatments are reported to improve hydrophobicity in some systems.
Natural oils can be incorporated into engineered bacterial-cellulose structures, but the outcome depends on surface modification, oil chemistry, loading, and drying history.
prohibited_inference: Oil automatically waterproofs untreated SCOBY biopapyrus.
Ancient Egyptians oiled papyrus sheets using the same process.
SCOBY itself is an oil-rich feedstock from which useful oil can simply be pressed.
The oil-processing overlap proves ancient bacterial-cellulose technology.

new_experimental_lane.purpose: Determine whether contact with a selected plant oil changes mass, flexibility, writing behavior, surface wetting, translucency, odor, tackiness, or long-term stability of a dried BioPapyrus sheet.

minimum_design.control: Untreated strip from the same dried sheet
minimum_design.test: Matched sacrificial strip exposed to a documented small quantity of a single known plant oil at room temperature
record: oil mass or applied amount if measurable
sample dry mass before and after
odor and visible oxidation/change over time

safety_boundary: No heating is required or authorized by this record.
Do not use unknown, toxic, volatile, or flammable solvent mixtures.
Do not return materials-test samples to food or beverage use.
Do not generalize from one oil to all oils.
new_experimental_lane.promotion_gate: Only call an oil treatment beneficial if matched controls and repeat samples show a reproducible improvement in a predefined property without unacceptable trade-offs.
